title: Science and Technology: Unit-wise Objective Question Bank
html:
Group A of the Science paper is ten one-mark items, and they are the fastest ten marks in the whole examination. They test a definition, a unit, a name, a one-step substitution or a misconception planted as a distractor.

This chapter drills all eleven units of the Grade 8 textbook in order. Each section opens with a facts line — what the one-mark items keep returning to — then gives eight items, then a key in which every answer carries its reason.

How to use this chapter

Do one section immediately after you read that chapter in the notes, and again in the last week. Cover the key with a sheet of paper. Mark yourself honestly: a half-remembered answer is a wrong answer in the hall.

2.1 Scientific Learning

Facts. Steps of the scientific method: observation → problem → hypothesis → experiment → analysis → conclusion. A hypothesis is a testable guess.

SI base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), kelvin (temperature), ampere (current). Volume of an irregular solid is found by water displacement.

  1. A tentative, testable explanation of an observation is called a [1]alawbtheorychypothesisdconclusion
  2. The SI base unit of temperature is the [1]adegree Celsiusbkelvincfahrenheitdjoule
  3. The variable the experimenter deliberately changes is the [1]adependent variablebindependent variableccontrolled variabledconstant
  4. Which instrument is used to find the volume of a small irregular stone? [1]aspring balancebmeasuring cylindercbeam balancedvernier scale
  5. A length of 3.5 km in metres is [1]a35 mb350 mc3500 md35000 m
  6. In an experiment on plant growth with light, the amount of water given to every pot is kept the same. Water here is a [1]adependent variablebindependent variableccontrolled variabledhypothesis
  7. The last step of the scientific method is [1]ahypothesisbexperimentcanalysis of datadconclusion
  8. Which of the following is not a quality of a good scientist? [1]acuriositybhonesty in recording datacaccepting claims without evidencedpatience
Answers

1. (c) — a hypothesis can be tested; a theory is already well tested.

2. (b) — the kelvin is the SI base unit; the degree Celsius is derived.

3. (b) — the independent variable is changed by the experimenter.

4. (b) — the rise in water level gives the displaced volume.

5. (c) — 3.5\times1000=3500 m.

6. (c) — a quantity deliberately held constant is a controlled variable.

7. (d) — the conclusion judges the hypothesis against the data.

8. (c) — science accepts a claim only with evidence.

2.2 Information and Communication Technology

Facts. ICT tools: ATM (Automated Teller Machine), photocopier (uses xerography and electrostatic charge), scanner (hard copy \rightarrow soft copy), printer (soft copy \rightarrow hard copy), router (forwards data using IP addresses), Wi-Fi (radio waves), set-top box (decodes digital TV signal).

Search engine (Google, Bing) finds web pages; browser (Chrome, Firefox) opens them; ISP (Nepal Telecom, WorldLink) provides internet access. Nepal's cyber law is the Electronic Transactions Act (ETA) 2063 BS.

Robotics (Sophia, Jia Jia), Virtual Reality (VR headset), Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Cloud Computing are emerging technologies.

  1. Which device converts a printed paper document (hard copy) into a digital file (soft copy)? [1]aprinterbmonitorcscannerdspeaker
  2. What does ATM stand for in banking? [1]aAutomatic Time MachinebAutomated Teller MachinecAdvanced Transfer MachinedAutomated Token Machine
  3. Which device receives a digital signal, decodes it and displays television channels on a TV? [1]aphotocopierbset-top box (STB)cscannerdcash dispenser
  4. Which of the following is a search engine? [1]aGoogle ChromebMozilla FirefoxcGoogledMicrosoft Word
  5. A company that provides internet access to homes and offices (such as Nepal Telecom or WorldLink) is called an [1]aURLbISPcATMdOCR
  6. Storing and accessing data and programs over remote internet servers instead of a local hard disk is called [1]axerographybcloud computingcvirtual realitydphotocopying
  7. Nepal's cyber law is the Electronic Transactions Act (ETA) enacted in [1]a2058 BSb2063 BSc2072 BSd2080 BS
  8. Sharing another person's photograph online without permission or sending threatening messages online is an example of [1]acomputer ethicsbcybercrime / cyberbullyingccloud storagedvirtual reality
Answers

1. (c) — a scanner is an input device that turns hard copy into soft copy.

2. (b) — Automated Teller Machine, used for 24-hour cash withdrawal and banking.

3. (b) — a set-top box decodes cable/optical-fibre/satellite TV signals.

4. (c) — Google is a search engine; Chrome and Firefox are web browsers.

5. (b) — Internet Service Provider (ISP).

6. (b) — cloud computing stores data on remote servers accessed via the internet.

7. (b) — the Electronic Transactions Act (ETA), 2063 BS (2006 AD).

8. (b) — it violates privacy and cyber law.

2.3 Living Beings and Their Structure

Facts. Cell: discovered by Robert Hooke (1665) in cork. Plant cells have a cell wall, large vacuole and chloroplasts; animal cells do not have a cell wall.

Mitochondrion is the powerhouse; ribosome makes protein; nucleus controls activity. Tissue → organ → organ system. Five kingdoms (Whittaker, 1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. Binomial nomenclature: Linnaeus.

  1. The cell was discovered by [1]aRobert HookebLeeuwenhoekcSchwanndWhittaker
  2. Which structure is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell? [1]anucleusbcell wallccytoplasmdmitochondrion
  3. The powerhouse of the cell is the [1]aribosomebnucleuscmitochondriondvacuole
  4. Organisms whose cells have no true nucleus belong to the kingdom [1]aProtistabMoneracFungidPlantae
  5. The cell wall of a fungus is made of [1]acellulosebchitinclignindpeptidoglycan
  6. In Oryza sativa, the word sativa denotes the [1]agenusbfamilycspeciesdorder
  7. A group of similar cells performing the same function is a [1]atissueborgancsystemdorganism
  8. Which one is a unicellular eukaryote? [1]abacteriumbAmoebacmushroomdfern
Answers

1. (a) — Hooke saw empty cork cells in 1665.

2. (b) — the rigid cellulose cell wall is a plant feature.

3. (c) — respiration releasing energy occurs in mitochondria.

4. (b) — Monera are prokaryotes.

5. (b) — chitin; cellulose belongs to plants.

6. (c) — the second word of a binomial is the species.

7. (a) — similar cells with one function form a tissue.

8. (b) — Amoeba is a single-celled protist with a true nucleus.

2.4 Biodiversity and Environment

Facts. Biodiversity = variety of life. Nepal occupies about 0.1 % of the world's land but has about 3.2 % of its known plant species and about 1.1 % of its animal species. Ecosystem = biotic + abiotic components.

Food chain: producer → herbivore → carnivore. Energy flows one way; only about 10 % passes to the next level. Causes of biodiversity loss: habitat destruction, poaching, pollution, invasive species, climate change.

  1. In a food chain, green plants are [1]aconsumersbproducerscdecomposersdparasites
  2. Which of these is an abiotic component of an ecosystem? [1]aearthwormbfunguscsunlightdgrass
  3. The approximate share of energy that passes from one trophic level to the next is [1]a1 %b10 %c50 %d90 %
  4. Organisms that break down dead bodies and return nutrients to the soil are [1]aproducersbherbivorescdecomposersdcarnivores
  5. Which is not a direct cause of biodiversity loss? [1]ahabitat destructionbpoachingcafforestationdinvasive species
  6. A one-horned rhinoceros is best conserved in [1]aChitwan National ParkbShey Phoksundo National ParkcSagarmatha National ParkdRara National Park
  7. In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the frog is a [1]aproducerbprimary consumercsecondary consumerddecomposer
  8. Mikania (lahare banmara) spreading in Nepal's forests is an example of [1]aan endemic speciesban invasive speciesca keystone speciesda producer at risk
Answers

1. (b) — they make food by photosynthesis.

2. (c) — sunlight is non-living.

3. (b) — roughly 10 %; the rest is lost mainly as heat.

4. (c) — decomposers recycle nutrients.

5. (c) — afforestation restores habitat.

6. (a) — Chitwan holds Nepal's largest rhinoceros population.

7. (c) — it eats the primary consumer, the grasshopper.

8. (b) — an introduced species spreading at the cost of native ones.

2.5 Life Process

Facts. Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide, water, chlorophyll and sunlight; it makes glucose and oxygen. Respiration releases energy from food; aerobic respiration needs oxygen, anaerobic does not.

Transpiration is loss of water as vapour, mainly through stomata. Digestion in humans: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine. Bile from the liver emulsifies fat.

Blood: red cells carry oxygen (haemoglobin), white cells defend, platelets clot.

  1. The raw materials of photosynthesis are [1]aglucose and oxygenbcarbon dioxide and watercoxygen and waterdglucose and carbon dioxide
  2. Loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant is [1]arespirationbtranspirationcguttationdtranslocation
  3. Most absorption of digested food takes place in the [1]astomachbsmall intestineclarge intestinedoesophagus
  4. The pigment that carries oxygen in blood is [1]achlorophyllbmelaninchaemoglobindinsulin
  5. Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces carbon dioxide and [1]alactic acidbethanolcglucosedwater only
  6. Bile is produced by the [1]apancreasblivercgall bladderdstomach
  7. The pores on a leaf through which gases are exchanged are [1]alenticelsbstomatachydathodesdveins
  8. During heavy exercise, muscle cramp is caused by the build-up of [1]aethanolblactic acidcglucosedurea
Answers

1. (b) — glucose and oxygen are the products, not the raw materials.

2. (b) — transpiration, mainly through stomata.

3. (b) — the villi of the small intestine absorb nutrients.

4. (c) — haemoglobin in red blood cells.

5. (b) — yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide (fermentation).

6. (b) — the liver makes bile; the gall bladder stores it.

7. (b) — stomata, guarded by guard cells.

8. (b) — anaerobic respiration in muscle forms lactic acid.

2.6 Force and Motion

Facts. Speed = distance ÷ time; velocity is speed with direction; acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time. Newton's first law: a body keeps its state unless a net force acts (inertia). Second law: F = ma.

Third law: equal and opposite reaction. Weight W = mg; g = 9.8 m/s² (often taken as 10 m/s²). Mass is in kilograms and does not change with place; weight is a force in newtons and does.

  1. The SI unit of force is the [1]akilogrambnewtoncjouledpascal
  2. A body of mass 5 kg is acted on by a force of 20 N. Its acceleration is [1]a100 m/s²b25 m/s²c4 m/s²d0.25 m/s²
  3. The weight of a 10 kg body where g = 9.8 m/s² is [1]a10 Nb98 Nc9.8 Nd980 N
  4. A passenger falls forward when a moving bus stops suddenly because of [1]ainertia of motionbinertia of restcfrictiondgravity
  5. A car covers 150 km in 3 hours. Its average speed is [1]a30 km/hb45 km/hc50 km/hd450 km/h
  6. A rocket moves forward because the exhaust gases are pushed backward. This illustrates [1]athe first lawbthe second lawcthe third lawdthe law of gravitation
  7. Which quantity does not change when a body is taken from the earth to the moon? [1]aweightbmasscacceleration due to gravitydgravitational force on it
  8. A body moving with uniform velocity has acceleration [1]auniform and positivebzerocincreasingdnegative
Answers

1. (b) — the newton.

2. (c) — a = F/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s².

3. (b) — W = mg = 10\times9.8 = 98 N.

4. (a) — the body tends to continue in motion.

5. (c) — 150/3 = 50 km/h.

6. (c) — action and reaction are equal and opposite.

7. (b) — mass is a constant quantity of matter.

8. (b) — uniform velocity means no change in velocity.

2.7 Energy in Daily Life

Facts. Heat travels by conduction (solids), convection (liquids and gases, sea/land breeze) and radiation (no medium needed, electromagnetic waves).

A thermos flask reduces heat loss by all three modes (vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered walls reduce radiation).

Concave mirrors converge light (real images except inside F; used in torches, headlights, shaving/dentist mirrors); convex mirrors diverge light (always virtual, erect, diminished image; used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles, R = 2f).

Sound wave speed v = f\lambda: infrasound (< 20\text{ Hz}), audible sound (20\text{ Hz}\text{–}20\text{ kHz}), ultrasound (> 20\text{ kHz}); sound intensity is measured in decibel (\text{dB}).

  1. Heat transfer from the sun to the earth through empty space occurs by [1]aconductionbconvectioncradiationdevaporation
  2. In a thermos flask, the vacuum between the double glass walls prevents heat transfer by [1]aradiation onlybconduction and convectioncreflectiondabsorption
  3. Which mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image and is used as a side rear-view mirror in vehicles? [1]aplane mirrorbconcave mirrorcconvex mirrordparabolic mirror
  4. If the radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 30\text{ cm}, its focal length is [1]a60\text{ cm}b30\text{ cm}c15\text{ cm}d10\text{ cm}
  5. Where is the image formed by a concave mirror when an object is placed at its centre of curvature (C)? [1]aat Fbat C, real, inverted and same sizecbehind the mirrordbeyond C
  6. What is the frequency range of audible sound for a normal human ear? [1]abelow 20\text{ Hz}b20\text{ Hz} to 20\text{ kHz}cabove 20\text{ kHz}d1\text{ Hz} to 100\text{ Hz}
  7. Sound waves of frequency greater than 20\text{ kHz} are called [1]ainfrasonic soundbultrasonic soundcaudible sounddsupersonic wave
  8. The intensity (loudness level) of sound is measured in [1]ahertz (\text{Hz})bdecibel (\text{dB})cpascal (\text{Pa})ddioptre (\text{D})
Answers

1. (c) — radiation travels as electromagnetic waves without requiring a material medium.

2. (b) — conduction and convection require a material medium and cannot cross a vacuum.

3. (c) — a convex mirror gives an erect, diminished image with a wide field of view.

4. (c) — f = R/2 = 30/2 = 15\text{ cm}.

5. (b) — an object at C forms a real, inverted image of the same size at C.

6. (b) — 20\text{ Hz} to 20,000\text{ Hz} (20\text{ kHz}).

7. (b) — ultrasound (> 20\text{ kHz}), used by bats, SONAR and ultrasonography.

8. (b) — decibel (\text{dB}).

2.8 Electricity and Magnetism

Facts. Lodestone (magnetite) is a natural magnet. Molecular theory of magnetism (Weber/Ewing): molecular magnets form closed chains in unmagnetised iron and open aligned chains in a magnet.

Heating, hammering or dropping causes demagnetisation; soft-iron keepers preserve magnets.

Terrestrial magnetism: the earth behaves like a giant magnet; angle of declination and angle of dip (inclination, 0^\circ at magnetic equator and 90^\circ at magnetic poles).

Household wiring is in parallel; fuse and MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker) are connected in the live (phase) wire; the longest, thickest pin of a 3-pin plug is the earth pin.

Energy in units (\text{kWh}) = P(\text{kW}) \times N \times t(\text{h}).

  1. According to the molecular theory of magnetism, in an unmagnetised iron bar the molecular magnets are arranged in [1]aparallel open chainsbrandom closed chainsca single straight linedonly at the centre
  2. The angle between the magnetic meridian and geographical meridian at a place is called the [1]aangle of dipbangle of declinationccritical angledangle of incidence
  3. What is the value of the angle of dip at the earth's magnetic poles? [1]a0^\circb45^\circc60^\circd90^\circ
  4. Which of the following causes demagnetisation of a permanent magnet? [1]astoring with soft-iron keepersbheating or hammering the magnetckeeping away from ACdcoating with paint
  5. In household wiring, a fuse or MCB is always connected in the [1]aneutral wirebearth wireclive (phase) wiredany wire
  6. What is the purpose of the longest and thickest top pin in a three-pin electrical plug? [1]ato carry live currentbto connect the appliance body to the earth wire for safetycto increase voltagedto act as a switch
  7. A 100\text{ W} bulb used for 10\text{ hours} consumes [1]a0.1\text{ unit}b1\text{ unit}c10\text{ units}d100\text{ units}
  8. Which modern safety device automatically trips a switch and can be reset without replacing a melted wire? [1]acartridge fusebMCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker)cammeterdvoltmeter
Answers

1. (b) — closed chains cancel each other's magnetic poles.

2. (b) — angle of declination.

3. (d) — a dip needle stands vertically (90^\circ) at the magnetic poles and horizontally (0^\circ) at the magnetic equator.

4. (b) — heating, hammering or dropping disturbs the alignment of molecular magnets.

5. (c) — the live (phase) wire, so the appliance is isolated from high potential when the circuit breaks.

6. (b) — earthing carries any leakage current safely to the ground before the live pins make contact.

7. (b) — 0.1\text{ kW} \times 10\text{ h} = 1\text{ kWh} = 1\text{ unit}.

8. (b) — MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker).

2.9 Matter

Facts. Atom: positively charged protons (p^+) and neutral neutrons (n^0) in the central nucleus; negatively charged electrons (e^-) revolve in shells K, L, M, N. Maximum electrons in the n-th shell = 2n^2 (K=2, L=8, M=18, N=32).

Valence electrons are electrons in the outermost shell; valency is combining capacity. Molecular formula is written by the criss-cross method.

Modern Periodic Law (Moseley): properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers (18 groups, 7 periods). Word equations and balanced chemical equations obey conservation of mass.

  1. Which sub-atomic particle is electrically neutral (chargeless) and located in the nucleus? [1]aprotonbelectroncneutrondpositron
  2. According to the 2n^2 rule, what is the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the M-shell (n = 3)? [1]a2b8c18d32
  3. What is the electronic configuration and valency of Magnesium (Z = 12)? [1]a2, 8, 1 and valency 1b2, 8, 2 and valency 2c2, 8, 3 and valency 3d2, 6 and valency 2
  4. By the criss-cross method, the molecular formula of calcium chloride (\text{Ca} valency 2, \text{Cl} valency 1) is [1]a\text{CaCl}b\text{Ca}_2\text{Cl}c\text{CaCl}_2d\text{Ca}_2\text{Cl}_2
  5. What is the molecular weight of water (\text{H}_2\text{O}), given \text{H} = 1\text{ amu} and \text{O} = 16\text{ amu}? [1]a17\text{ amu}b18\text{ amu}c20\text{ amu}d32\text{ amu}
  6. The modern periodic table developed by Henry Moseley is based on increasing [1]aatomic weightbatomic numbercneutron numberdvalency
  7. How many vertical groups and horizontal periods are there in the modern periodic table? [1]a8 groups, 7 periodsb18 groups, 7 periodsc7 groups, 18 periodsd16 groups, 8 periods
  8. As we move from top to bottom down a group in the periodic table, the number of shells and atomic size [1]adecreasebremain constantcincreasedbecome zero
Answers

1. (c) — the neutron has no charge (0) and mass 1\text{ amu}.

2. (c) — 2n^2 = 2 \times 3^2 = 18 electrons.

3. (b) — K=2, L=8, M=2; it loses 2 valence electrons so valency is 2.

4. (c) — exchanging valencies 2 and 1 gives \text{CaCl}_2.

5. (b) — 2 \times 1 + 16 = 18\text{ amu}.

6. (b) — atomic number (number of protons).

7. (b) — 18 groups and 7 periods.

8. (c) — a new shell is added at each step down a group, increasing atomic size.

2.10 Materials Used in Daily Life

Facts. Acids give \text{H}^+ ions in water, taste sour, turn blue litmus red and methyl orange red; bases give \text{OH}^- ions, taste bitter, turn red litmus blue, methyl orange yellow and phenolphthalein pink.

Acid + Base \rightarrow Salt + Water (neutralisation). Acid rain is caused by \text{SO}_2 and \text{NO}_2 dissolving in rain water to form \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 and \text{HNO}_3.

Temporary hardness of water is due to bicarbonates of \text{Ca} and \text{Mg} (removed by boiling or Clark's lime method); permanent hardness is due to chlorides and sulphates of \text{Ca} and \text{Mg} (removed by washing soda \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 or permutit).

Alloys: brass (\text{Cu} + \text{Zn}), bronze (\text{Cu} + \text{Sn}), steel (\text{Fe} + \text{C}), stainless steel (\text{Fe} + \text{Cr} + \text{Ni} + \text{C}).

  1. What colour does methyl orange indicator show in an acidic solution? [1]ayellowbred (pinkish-red)cbluedcolourless
  2. Which gases are the main causes of acid rain? [1]a\text{O}_2 and \text{N}_2b\text{SO}_2 and \text{NO}_2 (along with \text{CO}_2)c\text{H}_2 and \text{He}d\text{NH}_3 and \text{CH}_4
  3. Temporary hardness of water is caused by dissolved [1]achlorides of \text{Ca} and \text{Mg}bsulphates of \text{Ca} and \text{Mg}cbicarbonates of \text{Ca} and \text{Mg}dsodium chloride
  4. Which method can remove both temporary and permanent hardness of water? [1]aboiling onlybadding washing soda (\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) or permutit processcfiltration through clothddecantation
  5. Brass is an alloy of [1]acopper and tinbcopper and zincciron and carbondcopper and aluminium
  6. Bronze (used for statues, medals and bells) is an alloy of [1]acopper and tinbcopper and zincciron and nickeldlead and tin
  7. Which elements are mixed with iron and carbon to make rust-resistant stainless steel? [1]achromium and nickelbzinc and leadctin and silverdsulphur and phosphorus
  8. Which acid is present in vinegar and lemon juice respectively? [1]ahydrochloric acid and nitric acidbacetic acid and citric acidcsulphuric acid and carbonic aciddlactic acid and formic acid
Answers

1. (b) — methyl orange turns red in acid and yellow in base.

2. (b) — \text{SO}_2 and \text{NO}_2 form sulphuric and nitric acids in rainwater.

3. (c) — calcium bicarbonate \text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2 and magnesium bicarbonate \text{Mg(HCO}_3)_2.

4. (b) — washing soda and permutit precipitate or exchange \text{Ca}^{2+} and \text{Mg}^{2+} ions from both bicarbonates and chlorides/sulphates.

5. (b) — copper (\text{Cu}) + zinc (\text{Zn}).

6. (a) — copper (\text{Cu}) + tin (\text{Sn}).

7. (a) — chromium (\text{Cr}) and nickel (\text{Ni}).

8. (b) — vinegar contains acetic acid and citrus fruits contain citric acid.

2.11 The Earth and Universe

Facts. Minerals are naturally occurring homogeneous solids with definite chemical composition (metallic, non-metallic, energy minerals). Iron ore in Nepal: Phulchoki (Lalitpur) and Thoshe (Ramechhap); limestone: Udayapur, Chobhar.

Origin of earth hypotheses: Nebular (Kant–Laplace), Planetesimal, Tidal (Jeans–Jeffreys).

Geological eras: Precambrian, Palaeozoic (fishes, amphibians, ferns), Mesozoic (age of reptiles/dinosaurs), Cenozoic (age of mammals, humans and angiosperms). Big Bang theory explains the origin and expansion of the universe.

Minor bodies: asteroids (mostly between Mars and Jupiter), comets (icy nucleus, coma, tail pointing away from sun), meteoroids \rightarrow meteors (shooting stars) \rightarrow meteorites.

  1. Where is the famous Phulchoki iron ore deposit located in Nepal? [1]aRamechhapbLalitpurcUdayapurdMustang
  2. Which geological era is known as the "Age of Reptiles (Dinosaurs)"? [1]aPrecambrian erabPalaeozoic eracMesozoic eradCenozoic era
  3. Human beings (Homo sapiens) and modern mammals evolved in the [1]aPrecambrian erabPalaeozoic eracMesozoic eradCenozoic era
  4. The asteroid belt in our solar system lies mainly between the orbits of [1]aEarth and MarsbMars and JupitercJupiter and SaturndVenus and Earth
  5. Which part of a comet always points away from the sun due to solar wind and radiation pressure? [1]anucleusbcomactaildcore
  6. A fragment of rock from space that survives burning in the atmosphere and hits the earth's surface is called a [1]ameteoroidbmeteor (shooting star)cmeteoritedcomet
  7. Which theory is the most widely accepted scientific explanation for the origin of the universe? [1]aTidal hypothesisbNebular hypothesiscBig Bang theorydSteady state theory
  8. Which non-metallic mineral is the main raw material used in Udayapur and Hetauda cement factories? [1]ahaematiteblimestonecgraphitedgalena
Answers

1. (b) — Phulchoki is in Lalitpur district (Thoshe is in Ramechhap).

2. (c) — dinosaurs originated, dominated and went extinct in the Mesozoic era.

3. (d) — Cenozoic era (the current geological era).

4. (b) — between Mars and Jupiter.

5. (c) — the comet's tail is blown away from the sun by solar wind.

6. (c) — meteorite (in space: meteoroid; bright streak in air: meteor).

7. (c) — the Big Bang theory.

8. (b) — limestone (\text{CaCO}_3).

Scoring all ten

Across the eleven units above there are 88 items. If you can finish them in 45 minutes with 80 or more correct, Group A of your Science paper is secure. Below that, mark the units where you lost marks and re-read only those chapters — not the whole book.
